content: 1. Interferon-alpha therapy has been studied extensively for its role in treating chronic hepatitis C. Research from 1995 highlights its application and outcomes in this context. 2. Combination therapy using interferon and ribavirin has been evaluated as an initial treatment for chronic hepatitis C. A 1999 study discusses its effectiveness and potential benefits. 3. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) diagnostic tests, including their clinical use for diagnosis and monitoring during therapy, were reviewed in 1999. These tests are critical for managing chronic hepatitis C. 4. The AMPLICOR reverse transcription-PCR test for HCV RNA has been calibrated to international units, improving its genotype reactivity and performance characteristics. This advancement was documented in 2000. 5. A 1995 study found that the loss of serum HCV RNA at week 4 of interferon-alpha therapy is associated with better long-term outcomes in patients with chronic hepatitis C. 6. A comparison of three quantitative HCV RNA assays in 1998 demonstrated the importance of baseline viral load accuracy in predicting treatment outcomes for chronic hepatitis C. 7. A multicenter randomized controlled trial in 2003 compared daily induction combination therapy with alpha-2b interferon and ribavirin to standard combination therapy in treatment-naive chronic hepatitis C patients. 8. The initial decline in serum HCV RNA and its correlation with response to interferon-alpha therapy was quantified in a 1998 study, providing insights into treatment efficacy. 9. An inter-laboratory comparison of qualitative and quantitative HCV RNA detection methods in Italy in 2004 highlighted the variability in diagnostic virology practices. 10. Molecular diagnosis of viral hepatitis, including hepatitis C, was reviewed in 2002, emphasizing the importance of accurate and standardized diagnostic methods. 11. A 2002 study introduced an assay for quantifying HCV RNA in serum, further advancing diagnostic capabilities. 12. A 2003 study compared different HCV viral load and genotyping assays, providing insights into their relative accuracy and utility. 13. The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) published an international consensus statement on hepatitis C in 1999, outlining diagnostic and treatment guidelines. 14. Advances in the standardization of HCV RNA quantification were discussed in 2000, highlighting progress and remaining challenges in this area. 15. A 2009 study examined the impact of adherence to hepatitis C therapy on early virologic outcomes, emphasizing the importance of patient compliance. 16. Adherence to combination therapy was shown to enhance sustained virologic response in genotype-1-infected patients with chronic hepatitis C, as reported in a 2002 study. 17. The diagnostic landscape for hepatitis C technology was reviewed in 2016, focusing on the role of HCV core antigen testing as an alternative to nucleic acid testing (NAT) for detecting active HCV infection and monitoring treatment response. 18. HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) testing has been developed as a cost-effective and less centralized alternative to NAT. This systematic review aimed to assess the diagnostic accuracy of HCVcAg testing and its utility in monitoring treatment and confirming cure. 19. The Abbott ARCHITECT HCV Ag assay, a two-step automated chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay, is the most widely studied HCVcAg test. Other tests, such as the Fujirebio Lumipulse and EIKEN Lumispot, are also available in specific regions. 20. HCVcAg testing offers a potential alternative for monitoring treatment response and assessing sustained virologic response (SVR). 21. The systematic review included commercially available HCVcAg tests and compared their diagnostic accuracy to NAT. The review also evaluated the best testing strategies for identifying chronic HCV infection and monitoring treatment outcomes. 22. The review identified variability in the sensitivity and specificity of different HCVcAg tests, with some tests showing high accuracy for detecting active HCV infection. However, data on their use for treatment monitoring and cure assessment remain limited. 23. The findings underscore the need for further research to optimize HCV diagnostic and monitoring strategies, particularly in resource-limited settings where affordable and accessible testing is critical.
